findings.text: The first paragraph says what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. A newcomer can say what the project is and why it matters before scrolling.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable.

findings.text: The header links straight to the next steps, and that section gives a clone command, prerequisites, ./setup.sh and a first command to try. The reader knows what to do next.
findings.source: Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself.

findings.text: The title and heading are about firstmate, a different project, while the address is Athena's site. A newcomer may think they are on the wrong page until they read the second paragraph, which explains that this page is a sample study.
findings.source:
/

Athena explains how firstmate handles work

findings.text: The page explains why it shows a study of firstmate: it is a demonstration. But almost all of the page is firstmate detail, and nothing shows Athena's main product, a traced commit with its cost and verdict, so the main claim is described but not shown.
findings.source: A study is Athena's written reading of another software project, taken at one fixed commit ... to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it

findings.text: This link in the header is meant for the project owner. A newcomer is not told who the owner is or what these proposals are, so it is a confusing second call to action next to the real one.
findings.source: Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision.

findings.text: The middle of the page is a dense state machine full of internal terms such as exit 75, places-held, close-pending and transition ids. A newcomer who only wants to judge Athena will likely skim past it. The short "Start here" section does give a readable summary.
findings.source: Transitions (cards t1–t11), Counters ("places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11")

findings.text: The page says Athena is written in Rust, but the prerequisites do not mention a Rust toolchain, an AI account or API key, or which operating systems work. A newcomer cannot tell whether setup.sh handles these.
findings.source: Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm (to install Claude Code).

findings.text: The first command to try is concrete and short. It does not say which repository it acts on (presumably the current directory) or what it costs to run, and the page's own pitch puts cost first.
findings.source: Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog". ... press Enter to run it on your repository.

findings.text: The page is honest about its limits, which supports the traceability pitch. It also tells a newcomer that Athena's first pass missed several paths, and nothing says how those gaps were caught.
findings.source: f3 ... A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths: teardown reopening a backlog item ... local-only ships ... scouts ... and relaunch

findings.text: This points to a folder in a repository the reader has not seen and gives no link to it, so it does nothing for a newcomer.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
